sections.h2: Who do you call about a Marion County tax bill?
sections.html:
Two courthouse offices in Salem cover most questions: the Supervisor of Assessments and the Treasurer. The Supervisor of Assessments is at 100 E. Main St., Room 101, Salem, IL 62881, staffed on weekdays during the day, and answers at (618) 548-3853. The Treasurer is at 100 E. Main St., Suite 105, and takes calls at 618-548-3858.

The assessment office keeps a property record card on every parcel in the county. The card lists the characteristics being assessed, and the office also transfers ownership once a deed has been recorded with the Marion County Recorder. A change of mailing address has to be made in writing, either on the county's form or in person. If you are selling, send the new owner's tax bill address to this office as soon as the deed is recorded, so the next bill reaches the right person.

The assessment office states its own limits plainly: it values property and has no control over how much tax you pay. The taxing bodies on your bill decide what they need, and that sets the dollar amount.

sections.h2: Where can you pay taxes in Marion County?
sections.html:
Payment channels are a local bank, the mail, the web, a courthouse drop box or the counter in Salem. The Treasurer's list of authorized banks includes First Financial Bank, Farmer's State Bank, US Bank, Iuka State Bank, Kaskaskia Valley Credit Union, Kinmundy Bank, Marion County Saving Bank, FNB Patoka, People's National Bank, Midland States Bank, Gen Fed Credit Union and Peoples State Bank. A bank will not take payment without the payment stub and will not accept anything after the second installment due date.

  • Mail checks to Marion County Treasurer, 100 East Main, Room 105, P.O. Box 1025, Salem, IL 62881, payable to Marion County Collector.
  • Include the stub from the bottom of the bill. If you lost the bill, add $2.00 for homeowners or $5.00 for mortgage companies and banks to reprint it.
  • Write the parcel number on the check, date it with the current date, and write it for the full installment. The office cannot accept partial payments or post-dated checks.
  • A letter postmarked by the due date counts as paid on time.
  • The secure drop box is at the west entrance of the courthouse, checked daily, and anything dropped off after 4:30 in the afternoon posts the following business day.

Online, card payments run through the county's payment portal with a 2.25 percent fee plus $1.50 per transaction. An e-check costs a flat $2.00. None of that goes to the county. Personal checks are accepted until 30 days before the tax sale, and after that the Treasurer wants certified funds, which means cash, a cashier's check or a money order.

sections.h2: What exemptions does Marion County offer homeowners?
sections.html:
The Supervisor of Assessments lists several exemptions, each tied to a section of the Property Tax Code. Check that yours appears on your bill, because the office says the General Homestead has to be on the bill for a principal residence.

Marion County homestead exemptions as described on the Supervisor of Assessments exemptions page
ExemptionStatuteAmount or condition
General Homestead35 ILCS 200/15-175Up to $6,000 off assessed valuation
Senior Citizen Homestead35 ILCS 200/15-170$5,000 reduction; owner reaches 65 before year end of the taxing year
Senior Assessment Freeze35 ILCS 200/15-172Household income under $65,000; file initially by July 1, renew yearly
Homestead Improvement35 ILCS 200/15-180Exempts a new deck, garage, porch or addition for four years
Returning Veterans35 ILCS 200/15-167$5,000 off EAV for the year of return and the next year
Disabled Persons35 ILCS 200/15-168$2,000 off EAV; annual application by July 1

Disabled veterans have two further routes. A specially adapted house can be exempt up to $100,000 of assessed value, certified by the Illinois Department of Veterans' Affairs. The standard disabled veterans exemption is $2,500 at 30 to 49 percent service-connected disability, $5,000 at 50 to 69 percent, and full exemption at 70 percent or more, if total EAV stays under $250,000. Veterans must file yearly by July 1.

The Homestead Improvement exemption caps at $25,000 of assessed value, or $75,000 of fair cash value, per year. A Natural Disaster exemption covers a rebuilt principal residence, provided it is no larger than 110 percent of the original and is rebuilt within two years.

sections.h2: What if a Marion County assessment looks too high?
sections.html:
Begin with a conversation at the assessment office, where staff will explain how the value was reached and which exemptions apply. The office's own test is simple: would you sell for the market value shown on the bill, or higher? If not, gather evidence. The Board of Review is the formal route, and the filing dates are printed on the change of assessment notice, so keep that notice and ask the Supervisor's office to confirm the deadline for your township.

Ask the Supervisor of Assessments for your property record card before filing. A wrong square footage, bath count or year built is the easiest kind of error to prove. A recent sale, a closing statement or a professional appraisal supports a value claim, and photos plus assessments of nearby similar homes support an uniformity claim. If the county board's answer disappoints you, the state's Property Tax Appeal Board hears the next round.

Marion County has seventeen townships, and the county website lists the township assessors. A township assessor can often fix a data error faster than a formal appeal can.

sections.h2: What does the Census show about Marion County housing?
sections.html:
Marion County is a smaller, lower-value market than much of the state. About 36,382 people lived here as of July 2025 by Census Bureau estimate, a 3.6 percent decline since 2020. QuickFacts counts 17,396 housing units, where owners live in 74.7 percent of occupied homes. A typical home they own is valued at $103,000 for 2020-2024, half of households earn above $61,240, and rent runs about $794 a month at the midpoint.

  • Households: 15,512, at 2.33 people each.
  • Median owner costs: $1,206 with a mortgage and $522 without.
  • Mean commute: 21.1 minutes.
  • Permits for new building in 2025: only 12.

With only 12 permits in a year, the existing housing stock sets prices, and a buyer compares your house with other older homes, so condition matters more than new-build competition.

sections.h2: What is Marion County, and who lives where?
sections.html:
Marion County sits in the southern half of Illinois, an area known as Little Egypt. It was organized on January 24, 1823 from parts of Jefferson and Fayette counties and named for Revolutionary War General Francis Marion. Salem holds the courthouse and Centralia is the biggest city, and Centralia anchors the Centralia micropolitan area, which belongs to the St. Louis combined statistical area. The county covers 576 square miles, with 572 of them land.

The four incorporated cities are Centralia, Kinmundy, Salem and Wamac. The county borders Fayette, Clay, Wayne, Jefferson, Washington and Clinton counties. The southwest corner marks the intersection of the Baseline and the Third Principal Meridian, the starting point for the third survey of the Northwest Territory, marked by a boulder south of Centralia near U.S. 51. In Salem, July highs average 88 degrees and January lows 18, with the most rain in May.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Marion County property taxes in person?
faqs.a: At the Treasurer's office in the Marion County Courthouse, 100 East Main Street, Salem, on weekdays. There is also a secure drop box at the courthouse's west entrance. Bring the payment stub from your bill.

faqs.q: Can I make a partial payment in Marion County?
faqs.a: No. The Treasurer states it cannot accept partial payments, so a check has to cover the full installment, including any penalty or interest if you are late.

faqs.q: What is the Marion County online payment fee?
faqs.a: Cards carry a 2.25 percent convenience fee plus $1.50 per transaction, and an e-check costs a flat $2.00. The fees go to the payment processor, not to the county.

faqs.q: Which exemption applies to the home I live in?
faqs.a: The General Homestead Exemption, up to $6,000 of assessed valuation, applies to an owner-occupied principal residence. Seniors, veterans and disabled owners may qualify for more. Confirm each with the Supervisor of Assessments.

faqs.q: How much is a typical Marion County home worth?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau puts it at $103,000 for 2020-2024. Over the same years half of households earned more than $61,240, and 74.7 percent of occupied homes have their owner living there.
